subject: Egress translation proxy: FQDN ownership and firewall handshake
messages:
From: Carlos Mendez <carlos.mendez@acmehealth.com>
To: Logan Wright <logan.wright@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 29 Sep 2027 14:12:00 -0700
Subject: [ACME -> Redwood] Clarify allowlisting model traffic for private connectors

Hi Logan / Marissa,

Quick question from our networking team as we prep the Private deployment: our perimeter allows outbound by FQDN/SNI (we do NOT want to maintain large IP allowlists if avoidable). Does Redwood require static IPs for model-serving egress from private endpoints, or can we safely rely on FQDN-based allowlisting / SNI pass-through to permit model traffic?

We also want to understand port ranges, whether TLS inspection will break responses, and how failover to a secondary region would look from an allowlist perspective.

Attached is our standard outbound policy for reference (see networks@acmehealth.com). Thanks — Carlos

--
Carlos Mendez
Director, Network Architecture
Acme Health
From: Logan Wright <logan.wright@redwood.ai>
To: Carlos Mendez <carlos.mendez@acmehealth.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>, David Kim <david.kim@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 30 Sep 2027 09:40:00 -0700
Subject: Re: [ACME -> Redwood] Clarify allowlisting model traffic for private connectors

Carlos — thanks for the clear question. High-level answer: Redwood Private can work with either approach, but there are tradeoffs. Below is a concise decision map plus concrete next steps we recommend for your environment.

Summary (short):
- Control-plane/management calls (telemetry, billing checks, control APIs) must reach our control plane and are best allowlisted by static IP ranges we provide.
- Model-serving egress (token generation, KV cache fetches, etc.) can be negotiated two ways:
  1) Customer-managed outbound proxy / translation (preferred). You allow a small set of egress FQDNs and the proxy maintains persistent TLS sessions to Redwood; the proxy exposes a stable outbound IP (your NAT) that you can manage.
  2) Redwood-managed NAT (fallback): we can provide a signed CSV of ephemeral egress IPs for your firewall. This is operationally simpler but means you must update allowlists for rotations.

Technical details and guidance:
- FQDN / SNI: If you rely on FQDN/SNI allowlisting, ensure the perimeter does SNI passthrough for TLS to avoid active TLS interception. TLS MITM (inspection) will break certificate pinning and response verification for our runtime; it is incompatible with end-to-end TLS between your proxy and Redwood.
- Ports: outbound to our services uses TCP 443 for control and serving. If you prefer to allow ranges, allow 443/TCP and ephemeral high-numbered ports for proxy source NAT.
- Keepalives / long-lived streams: streaming responses use persistent connections. Any intermediate proxy should be tuned with higher idle timeouts (suggest: 15m+) and support connection reuse.
- Failover / multi-region: if you plan to accept traffic routed to a secondary region, either: (a) configure your proxy to open outbound sessions to both regional FQDNs (recommended), or (b) update firewall rules to include Redwood failover egress IPs. If you use FQDN allowlisting, ensure both regional hostnames are included.

Concrete next steps we suggest:
1) Select approach: customer outbound proxy OR Redwood-managed NAT.
2) If proxy: share your proxy egress IP(s) and we will provide an example TLS config and streaming keepalive snippet (attached).
3) If Redwood NAT: we will provide an IP pack CSV (attached) and a weekly rotation schedule plus a webhook to notify you prior to changes.
4) Security: if you require mTLS to our control plane, we can enable client certs for control-plane endpoints (coordinate with David). Model-serving mTLS is available as an add-on but is uncommon since we recommend customer-side proxying for tenant isolation.

I've attached a preliminary egress IP pack (for the Redwood-managed NAT option) and a proxy config snippet you can paste into your outbound gateway. Kimberly / David, please add any constraints I missed.

Cheers,
Logan

Attachments: egress-ip-pack-20271003.csv; egress-proxy-config-snippet.txt
From: Carlos Mendez <carlos.mendez@acmehealth.com>

Date: Fri, 01 Oct 2027 11:18:00 -0700
Subject: Re: [ACME -> Redwood] Clarify allowlisting model traffic for private connectors

Thanks Logan — helpful summary. A few follow-ups from the networking team (copied):

- Port confirmation: so 443 outbound only for the service endpoints (we don't need to open any additional inbound ports to our private runtime), correct?
- mTLS: we prefer to enable mTLS for control-plane calls (auditing requirement). Is there a documented handshake and cert rotation cadence?
- Failover behavior: if Redwood rotates NAT IPs, how much lead time do you provide and is there an automated API we can poll to retrieve the new list (we'd like to script updates into our firewall appliance)?

On the allowlist model: our security policy forbids TLS MITM for healthcare workloads, so we'll do SNI passthrough + proxy translation on our side if that keeps us out of large IP maintenance. If Redwood enables a webhook for IP rotations, we can take the Redwood-managed NAT option as fallback.

Cheers,
Carlos

From: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.ai>
To: Carlos Mendez <carlos.mendez@acmehealth.com>

Subject: Re: [ACME -> Redwood] Clarify allowlisting model traffic for private connectors

Carlos — quick security notes and proposed SLA for change notifications:

1) Ports: correct — outbound to Redwood service endpoints is TCP/443. No inbound ports to your runtime are required.

2) mTLS: we support mutual TLS for control-plane endpoints. The flow: we issue a short-lived client cert (rotated every 30 days) and provide an automated enrollment endpoint. We can increase rotation to a shorter cadence if you need — David will run the cert rotation job and provide logs to your security team.

3) IP rotation / webhook: if you select Redwood-managed NAT we will:
   - Publish an authenticated webhook subscription that posts a signed rotation payload 7 days prior to any IP changes.
   - Maintain an API endpoint (/egress/ips) returning the current canonical CSV (HMAC-signed). You may poll this endpoint programmatically.

4) Operational recommendations:
   - If you use customer proxy translation, configure health checks to detect sticky sessions and enable dual-homing to both regions' FQDNs for a graceful failover.
   - We recommend a 10-minute overlap window during NAT rotations where old IPs remain valid while new ones come online to avoid connection churn.

If that matches your controls, we're prepared to proceed: option A (customer proxy) is lowest-maintenance for you and lowest-risk for end-to-end TLS. Option B (Redwood NAT) is acceptable if you prefer Redwood to manage egress IPs — we'll keep the webhook/APIs described above.

I'll drop a lightweight checklist below for your firewall team to sign-off and propose a short call to finalize the proxy config.

Firewall/egress checklist (for Acme Health sign-off):
- [ ] Permit outbound TCP/443 to the following FQDNs: models-us.redwood.ai, models-eu.redwood.ai (or allow by wildcard under redwood.ai if policy permits)
- [ ] If using Redwood NAT: import egress-ip-pack-20271003.csv into firewall and subscribe to webhook notifications
- [ ] Ensure SNI passthrough / no TLS MITM for model-serving flows
- [ ] Configure proxy keepalive >= 15m and connection reuse for streaming
- [ ] Enable mTLS for control-plane endpoints (coordinate cert enrollment)

Propose we run a 30-minute technical handshake on Tue Oct 5th to validate proxy configuration and cert enrollment. Logan / Kimberly, can you take the invite?

— David

----
David Kim
Head of Security Operations, Redwood Inference
